name: Lambda (batch + speed)
description: Lambda runs two parallel paths over the same source events: a batch layer that periodically recomputes accurate, complete views over the full history on the lake, and a speed layer that maintains approximate, low-latency views over recent events. A serving layer merges them so queries see both deep history and the last few seconds. The pattern's honest cost is dual implementation — the same logic exists twice, in batch code and streaming code, and keeping them consistent is a permanent tax. Modern table formats and real-time OLAP stores have eaten much of Lambda's original motivation, but the shape survives where batch recomputation over massive history must coexist with real-time freshness and neither path can be compromised.
when_to_use: Choose this when you need both provably-correct results over years of history (batch recomputation as the error-correction mechanism) and seconds-fresh views, and a single system cannot deliver both — common in metrics platforms, billing/usage analytics, and large-scale monitoring.
It also fits brownfield reality: a solid batch platform already exists and real-time is being added alongside rather than instead.
You must serve both years of history and the last few seconds in one answer.
when_not_to_use: Do not start here greenfield — evaluate Kappa (5) or a real-time OLAP store with batch backfill (8) first, as either avoids maintaining duplicate logic.
If 'real-time' actually means minutes, micro-batch on the existing batch stack is far cheaper.
The dual-codebase tax compounds with every metric added, so avoid Lambda when the metric surface is broad and fast-changing.

hot_spots.title: Dual codebases
hot_spots.detail: Batch and speed implement the same logic twice and inevitably drift apart.

hot_spots.title: Serving merge
hot_spots.detail: Incorrect merge windows double-count or drop events at the batch/speed boundary.

hot_spots.title: Batch latency
hot_spots.detail: Errors fixed only by recomputation wait for the next batch cycle.

evolution.reason: Collapse the dual codebases into a single streaming path.
A real-time OLAP store with batch backfill replaces both layers for query serving.

stages.name: Master dataset
stages.role: Immutable, append-only store of every raw event — the batch layer recomputes from it
stages.rationale: Cheap immutable object storage as the landing layer decouples ingestion from processing: replays, backfills, and audits read the raw dump instead of re-extracting from sources.

stages.name: Batch layer
stages.role: Periodically recompute complete, accurate views over full history on the lake
stages.rationale: Spark over lake storage (Parquet/Iceberg) is the proven engine for full-history recomputation — it scales to the scan volumes involved and shares infrastructure with the rest of a lakehouse. The batch layer's job is correctness: it silently fixes whatever the speed layer got wrong. Trino fits when recomputation is expressible as SQL and you already run it for interactive queries; EMR and Databricks are the managed places to run the Spark itself.

stages.name: Speed layer
stages.role: Maintain low-latency incremental views over events the batch layer has not yet processed
stages.rationale: Flink's event-time windowing and managed state fit the speed layer's job — incremental aggregates over the recent window, tolerating that batch will overwrite them with the truth later. Approximation is acceptable here by design, which relaxes the exactly-once pressure that makes streaming hard elsewhere. Kafka Streams keeps it library-simple inside JVM services; Spark Structured Streaming minimizes the dual-stack problem by sharing the batch engine's APIs — a real argument if you chose Spark for batch; Materialize replaces hand-built incremental logic with maintained SQL views.

stages.name: Serving merge
stages.role: Store both view sets and answer queries that merge historical and real-time results
stages.rationale: Druid was practically designed for Lambda serving — native dual ingestion (batch index jobs from the lake plus streaming from Kafka) with automatic segment replacement, so the batch layer's corrected history transparently supersedes speed-layer data without query-time merge logic. Pinot offers the same hybrid-table pattern with a more modern architecture; ClickHouse can play the role with materialized views plus batch inserts but leaves the merge semantics to you; StarRocks when joins at serve time matter. The segment-replacement mechanics are the whole trick — pick a store where they are first-class.
